purify

PYOOR-uh-fy -- Latin purus, 'clean, unmixed,' plus -fy, 'to make': to make pure. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To purify is to remove contaminants from something.

Villagers boil the river water to purify it before anyone takes a drink.

Example

An engineer runs cloudy well water through layers of sand, charcoal, and fine mesh until what drips out the other end is perfectly clear and safe to drink.

Removing contaminants until something is clean is exactly what it means to purify. Unlike 'dilute,' which only weakens impurities by adding more liquid, purify actually takes the impurities out.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

distill: To distill is to purify a liquid in one specific way: boiling it and catching the condensed vapor while impurities stay behind. Purify names the goal -- contaminants removed -- while distill names one exacting method of getting there.

filter: To filter is to remove particles by passing something through a barrier that traps them -- a screen, sand, charcoal. Filtering is one common way to purify, but purify is the larger claim: that what comes out is genuinely clean.

disinfect: To disinfect is to kill the germs on something, usually with chemicals -- the germs die where they are, and nothing is carried away. To purify is to take impurities out altogether, the way charcoal pulls grit and odor from water.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

contaminate: to make something impure or unsafe

pollute: to make dirty or harmful

Where it sits · how completely every taint is driven out — cleanse → purify → refine

cleanse vs. purify: Cleanse is broader and often gentler than purify -- you can cleanse a surface or a wound, while purify insists that contaminants are removed until something is truly pure.

refine vs. purify: Refine goes further than purify: to purify is to get the contaminants out, while to refine is to keep working the material -- pass after pass -- until it reaches its most perfect, finished form.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — pur-

root — pur-: pure, clean, unmixed (Latin (purus))

suffix — -ify

suffix — -ify: to make (Latin (facere, 'to make'))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin purus meant 'clean, unmixed,' and the -ify ending, from facere ('to make'), turns it into an action -- to purify is literally 'to make pure,' the same root behind pure and purity.
